analysis.title: US macro: FAQs to forecasts
key_insights: UBS CIO expects a three-hike Fed cycle: after September's 25bps hike, further hikes in December 2026 and March 2027, for 75bps of total tightening, moving policy into modestly restrictive territory.

September inflation surprised to the upside. Headline CPI rose to 3.7% y/y and core CPI to 2.6%, with firmer energy and underlying pressures. Core PCE is tracking near 3.1%, which signals stalled progress.
Q3 GDP is tracking near 3.2%, led by consumption and business investment rather than inventories or trade. First-half 2026 GDP growth was revised up to 2.4%.

Growth is expected to cool toward about 2% through 2027 as fiscal policy turns into a modest headwind and consumption moderates from a pace ahead of income growth. Continued AI investment supports the 2% level.

Tariff effects have largely faded and favorable base effects should help in early 2027. Rents and wage growth are broadly consistent with the Fed's target, supporting gradual disinflation toward mid-2027.

Risks favor additional tightening if inflation persists. AI demand and Middle East supply bottlenecks are upside inflation risks. Weaker AI capex or equity markets would weigh on investment and consumption.
UBS's oil price forecasts imply a 0.2-0.4pp drag on growth, but activity momentum before the Middle East conflict was strong and above trend.
Tariff rates fell about 3pps after the Supreme Court IEEPA ruling and the 10% Section 122 tariff. New Section 232 and 301 tariffs should be more durable, keeping tariff rates in a 10-15% range.
Job growth is volatile but the underlying 3-month trend is around 50k, about the breakeven rate for stable unemployment. Unemployment has stabilized and wage growth is cooling.
Consumption remains solid, supported by wealth gains among higher-income households and tax cuts, despite slow real income growth. OBBBA tax cut gains could be fully offset by higher energy costs.
AI capex has added about 0.5pp to growth over the past year. Investment is broadening, with manufacturing PMIs stronger and non-tech durables and equipment spending catching up to tech in 2Q and 3Q.

Chair Warsh cited strong activity, inflation trends, the share of inflation over 3%, and Middle East supply bottlenecks and oil product prices as supporting the case for tightening. He also said financial conditions were not restrictive.

UBS says 100bps of hikes cuts GDP by about 40bps after one year, and a 75bps cycle could reduce growth by roughly 20bps. Effects show up with a 1-2 quarter lag, mainly through investment and consumption.
Market pricing (forwards) embeds more hikes than UBS's forecast of two more.
Business output per hour is growing about 1pp above the 2010-2019 average of 1.2%. Estimates of AI's labor productivity effect over a decade center on 0.5-1.5%.

More than 20% of firms report using AI, firm-count weighted (Census survey). AI's estimated effect on the unemployment rate is about 0.2 percentage points or less, with weaker job growth for high-exposure and younger workers.
AI is adding to inflation through goods (software and computers), portfolio management services and electricity services.

The K-shaped consumer reflects high-income households benefiting from wealth gains and relatively lower inflation, while low-income households face higher inflation. The top 20% spending share appears to be rising.
The CBO deficit is expected to stay around 6-6.5% of GDP, with debt over 100% of GDP and rising 20pps by 2036. CBO estimates about 2bps higher long-term yields per 1pp of debt-to-GDP.
